name: Tanana Athabaskan, Minto and Salcha dialects

PhD dissertation, University of Washington. xv+329 pp. Alaska Native Language Archive item TN990T1998b,https://uafanlc.alaska.edu/Online/TN990T1998b/TN990T1998bf.2.PDF.Concurring: Tuttle, Siri G. 2000 [publ. 2003]. catalog_quote: [p.189] Both Salcha and Minto show evidence for quantity-sensitivity; a light syllable is only stressed when it precedes another light syllable. I will claim here, therefore, that Tanana stress is rhythmically trochaic. Heavy syllables are those which contain full vowels or are closed by a consonant. [pp.202-203] Specifically, I find that stems are preferentially stressed even when the syllabification pattern of a form renders them light syllables. Some suffixes and clitics are stressless even though they are heavy syllables; others are always stressed. Stressed suffixes and clitics are those which are tonally marked. [p.218] In a Tanana word with more than one stress, one stress is promoted to the status of Head of Prosodic Word and bears stronger stress. In Salcha and Minto, the head of a prosodic word is the rightmost stressed syllable. In both dialects, compound and phrasal stress is also rightmost. [p.219] So wherever a stem is word-final, it will be promoted, but where it is followed by a tonal suffix, this suffix will carry word stress. [pp.221-222] Prominence, which has slightly different acoustic correlates in the two languages, is assigned to heavy syllables (syllables with bimoraic vowels and closed syllables), to stems, and to syllables which bear tone. The metrical pattern is defined by the moraic trochee.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Lower Tanana (lowe1425) is not in the catalog. Of the four title hits, two are first-hand word-stress sources by Siri Tuttle and both were read in full from open ANLA copies already held by the project from the earlier reading today: the 1998 UW dissertation (Ch.5 'Stress', pp.180-224, scanned) and the 2003 Anthropological Linguistics paper (read as the Oct-2000 ANLA preprint typescript TN990T2003; the published AL 45(3):316-336 has no Crossref DOI and is JSTOR-only). Both state the same system for the Minto and Salcha dialects: stress on every heavy syllable (full vowel or closed syllable), on the first of two open reduced-vowel syllables (moraic trochee, right-edge anchored), always on the stem, on tonal suffixes only; primary stress is the rightmost stress (normally the stem), compounds right-headed; duration is the chief acoustic correlate. Leer 1976 (newly downloaded from ANLA, 86 image-only pp., first 6 scanned) is a comparative Athabaskan tonogenesis manuscript in which Lower Tanana is one of eleven daughter languages -- prosody but not word stress, priority none. 'Place Names and Stress Check' resolves to ANLA sound recording ANLC2556 (Lower Tanana, no author/date, no online file, no description in the API record) -- unclear/unread, low priority. Ancillary items held by the project from the earlier reading agree: Tuttle's 1997 LSA poster gives the one-line rule 'Stress falls on stems, full vowels, closed syllables, and on the first of two open reduced-vowel syllables'; Milanowski & Milanowski 1959 (Nenana dialect) only notes 'phonetic stress has been noted. No phonemic analysis has been made'. Best statement for a new catalog entry: Tuttle 1998 diss. pp.218 and 221-222 (file, pdf-pages 102, 105-106). New files and records logged; all look-ups were done with direct download/automated download against Glottolog, Crossref, ANLA API and ANLA online store.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable from morphology plus syllable weight: every stem is stressed; every heavy syllable (full/long vowel or closed syllable) is stressed; in strings of light (open, reduced-vowel) prefix syllables moraic trochees are built leftward from the stem foot, so a light syllable is stressed only when it precedes another light syllable and never immediately before the stem; lexically tonal suffixes/enclitics (Minto low or high-rising tone) are stressed, non-tonal suffixes/enclitics are stressless even if heavy. Primary (word) stress is the rightmost stressed syllable, i.e. the stem when it is word-final, otherwise a following tonal suffix; compound and phrasal stress are likewise rightmost. Duration is the main acoustic correlate; F0 is not a stress correlate in (sparsely tonal) Minto.
new_statements.secondary_stress: All non-rightmost stresses (heavy prefix syllables, heads of light-light trochees in the prefix string, non-final stems in compounds) surface as weaker stresses; adjacent stresses are tolerated; in connected speech non-primary stresses are often reduced but remain durationally distinct (§5.3.2.2 p.199, §5.5).
new_statements.exceptions: Some heavy suffixes/enclitics (e.g. nominalizers -en, -i; Salcha possessed-noun suffix) are lexically stressless (Nonfinality >> WSP); Minto possessed suffix -a' (tonal) is always stressed and takes word stress, so Minto possessive compounds have final-syllable main stress while Salcha has it on the rightmost stem (p.220); a few disyllabic nouns follow phonological rather than morphological structure (e.g. Minto ts'eba 'spruce' with final stress, p.191); word-final schwa is banned in Minto but allowed (unstressed) in Salcha, giving Minto final vs Salcha penultimate stress in cognate CeCe nouns (pp.190-192).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the (prosodic) word including conjunct prefixes, stem and suffixes/enclitics; analysis based on elicited citation forms checked against the consultant plus duration/F0/amplitude measurements of 1961 (Minto, Teddy Charlie) and 1974 (Salcha, Bessie Barnabas) text recordings, phrase-final syllables excluded from the word-position duration test. Author states Minto (Lower Tanana proper) and Salcha have the identical stress system; Minto additionally has sparse lexical low tone.
new_statements.identity_note: Tuttle's 'Tanana' covers two dialects she treats as one language with one stress system: Minto(-Nenana), i.e. Lower Tanana proper (lowe1425, ISO taa; consultant Isabel Charlie, texts of Teddy Charlie 1961), and Salcha(-Goodpaster) 'Middle/Transitional Tanana' (extinct 1993, last speaker Eva Moffit), which Kari and others sometimes separate from Lower Tanana as 'Middle Tanana'. The quoted rule is stated explicitly for both; differences are lexical (Minto has sparse low tone and bans word-final schwa). Milanowski 1959 describes the Nenana variety of the same language.

new_statements.reading: Lower Tanana (both Minto and Salcha) has a weight-sensitive, morphologically anchored stress system, not a fixed-position one: every heavy syllable (full vowel or closed syllable) is stressed; light open reduced-vowel syllables are stressed only as the first of two lights (moraic trochees built from the right edge of the prosodic word); the stem is always stressed even when made light by a vowel-initial suffix; suffixes/enclitics are stressed only when tonal; primary (word) stress falls on the rightmost stressed syllable, in practice the stem or a following tonal suffix, and compounds are also right-headed. For a catalog's classification this is 'stem-stress / weight-sensitive with rightmost primary' (right-edge oriented, unbounded within the word rather than fixed penult/final), with Minto and Salcha sharing one ranking and differing only in which suffixes carry tone. Instrumental support: duration is the primary correlate in both dialects (pp.183-187) and full-vowel duration in stressed syllables rises toward the word-final stressed syllable (Table 43, p.218-219). Tuttle 2003 (AL) restates the same rules from the same author and confirms them on archival narrative tapes; the 1997 LSA poster held by the project (TN990T1997a, p.3) gives the one-line version 'Stress falls on stems, full vowels, closed syllables, and on the first of two open reduced-vowel syllables.'

tone_statements.quote: Following Gussenhoven (2004), I assume that a language can be called "tonal" but demonstrate a low density of tonal marking. Among the low-toned languages, some are densely marked (Navajo) and some very sparsely marked (Lower Tanana). [...] In Lower Tanana, syllables ending in glottal stop bear low tone, as do syllables that historically, but not synchronically, ended in ejectives. [...] Looked at from the Athabascanist point of view, the phonetics support the traditional distinction between Lower Tanana (tone) and Ahtna (no tone), but I suggest that the comparison remains a useful, microtypological case for discussion of where the "tonal" boundary should be drawn.

sources.tag: read: notes on stress
sources.quote: Stress in Tanana is assigned based on morphology and on syllable quantity. All stems are stressed; all full vowels are stressed; all closed syllables are stressed, whether or not they contain a full vowel; and open syllables with reduced vowels may be stressed if they are followed by another open syllable. ... Stems bear primary stress, so that (6a) and (6c), which have two stresses, have main stress rightmost, on the stem. [p.11] ... heavy syllables stressed, light syllables stressed only if they precede another light syllable, never a light syllable stressed before a heavy. [p.12]

sources.quote: One of the major purposes of this paper is to formulate a hypothesis of the development of tone in modern Athabaskan from an earlier (pre-Proto-Athabaskan) system of vowel nuclei. ... In the case of Athabaskan, however, the development of tone depended not only on the vowel nucleus, but on the final consonant of the syllable. If the final consonant was glottalized, the reflex of the tone is opposite of what it is if the final consonant was not glottalized.
sources.note: Comparative-historical tonogenesis paper ('suprasegmentals' = tone from constricted vowel nuclei and glottalized stem-finals across Athabaskan, Eyak, Tongass Tlingit). Lower Tanana appears only as one of the daughter languages supplying cognate tone reflexes. Nothing on word-stress placement in the pages read; not a stress source.
